title: Sparling: End-to-End Spatial Concept Learning via Extremely Sparse Activations
claim: Only inputs and outputs are observed in training; the sparse intermediate representation linking them must be recovered end-to-end.
layout: 2 stacked rows, left-to-right X→M→Y, braces marking training-visible stages
description: Two horizontal rows, (a) a synthetic digit task and (b) an RNA splicing task, each following the same X → M → Y flow. In row (a), a noisy black-and-white 120x120 image holds faint digits. A large arrow labeled g* leads to a gray noise map where each digit is marked by a colored box and dot. A second arrow labeled h* leads to the output string 072634. Row (b) shows an RNA sequence line, then a line with colored protein-binding-site blocks, then a line with red and blue splice-site ticks. Dimension labels sit under each stage. Braces under the columns read 'Included in training' in blue for X and Y, and 'Not included in training' in pink for the middle M. The eye goes first to the large noisy image and the colored digit boxes.
caption: (a) Example of the DIGITCIRCLE domain, alongside (b) a cartoon of the splicing problem. The input x is mapped by the ground truth g∗function to the motif map m∗of the positions of every digit/protein binding sites, which is itself mapped by the ground truth h∗function to the output y∗, the sequence 072634/splice sites. Only x and y∗are available during training; the goal is to reconstruct g∗and h∗. Note that in splicing, unlike DIGITCIRCLE, the motifs can overlap. The M dots indicate the representation as described in Section 2, which is a one-hot encoding at each location.
abstract: Real-world processes often contain intermediate state that can be modeled as an extremely sparse activation tensor. In this work, we analyze the identifiability of such sparse and local latent intermediate variables, which we call motifs. We prove our Motif Identifiability Theorem, stating that under certain assumptions it is possible to precisely identify these motifs exclusively by reducing end-to-end error. Notably, we do not assume identifiability of parameters, but rather of a latent intermediate representation output by a local model, thus allowing these representations to be arbitrarily complex functions of the input. Additionally, we provide the Sparling algorithm, which uses a new kind of informational bottleneck that enforces levels of activation sparsity unachievable using other techniques. We confirm empirically that extreme sparsity is necessary to achieve good intermediate state modeling. On synthetic domains, we are able to precisely localize the intermediate states up to feature permutation with $>90\%$ accuracy, even though we only train end-to-end.
